questions.q: As per the book, consent before a procedure must contain all of the following components EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Components of consent = identification, diagnosis, planned procedure, surgeon, description, patient-specific complications, procedure-specific complications, benefits, alternate procedure and sign of patient, surgeon and witness. (Book p1)

questions.q: Which of the following is an explicit component of consent?
questions.exp: The planned procedure and the surgeon are explicit components of consent. (Book p1)

questions.q: A procedure-specific complication must be explained to the patient when its incidence is:
questions.exp: Procedure specific complications = any complication > 1% incidence. (Book p1)

questions.q: In addition to the planned procedure, consent must also discuss:
questions.exp: Consent includes benefits and the alternate procedure. (Book p1)

questions.q: The consent form is signed by:
questions.exp: Consent requires the sign of patient, surgeon and witness. (Book p1)

questions.q: In the color-coding of IV cannulas, the YELLOW cannula corresponds to gauge:
questions.exp: Yellow = 24G (max flow 13 (10) ml/min), the narrowest cannula in the chart. (Book p1)

questions.q: The BLUE IV cannula corresponds to gauge:
questions.exp: Blue = 22G with a maximal flow of 31 (30) ml/min. (Book p1)

questions.q: The PINK IV cannula corresponds to gauge:
questions.exp: Pink = 20G with a maximal flow of 67 (60) ml/min. (Book p1)

questions.q: The GREEN IV cannula corresponds to gauge:
questions.exp: Green = 18G with a maximal flow of 96 ml/min. (Book p1)

questions.q: The GRAY IV cannula corresponds to gauge:
questions.exp: Gray = 16G with a maximal flow of 236 (240 ml/min). (Book p1)

questions.q: The ORANGE IV cannula, which is used in shock, corresponds to gauge:
questions.exp: Orange (used in shock) = 14G, the widest cannula, with a maximal flow of 270 ml/min. (Book p1)

questions.q: The narrowest cannula in the color chart is:
questions.exp: The chart runs from narrow 24G (yellow) to wide 14G (orange). (Book p1)

questions.q: The widest cannula in the color chart is:
questions.exp: 14G orange is the widest cannula and is the one used in shock. (Book p1)

questions.q: The maximal flow rate of the 16G gray cannula is:
questions.exp: Gray 16G maximal flow = 236 (240 ml/min). (Book p1)

questions.q: The maximal flow rate of the 20G pink cannula is:
questions.exp: Pink 20G maximal flow = 67 (60) ml/min. (Book p1)

questions.q: The maximal flow rate of the 14G orange cannula is:
questions.exp: Orange 14G (used in shock) has the highest maximal flow of 270 ml/min. (Book p1)

questions.q: In the color chart, which group of cannulas is bracketed for paediatric patients?
questions.exp: Yellow (24G), blue (22G) and pink (20G) are grouped together for paediatric patients. (Book p1)

questions.q: A cannula with a maximal flow of 96 ml/min is color-coded:
questions.exp: Green = 18G with maximal flow 96 ml/min. (Book p1)

questions.q: The most common complication of an IV line is:
questions.exp: Superficial thrombophlebitis is the m/c complication of IV lines. (Book p1)

questions.q: Superficial thrombophlebitis at a cannulation site presents with:
questions.exp: Features of superficial thrombophlebitis: tender, cord-like swelling. (Book p1)

questions.q: The management of superficial thrombophlebitis at a cannula site is:
questions.exp: Management of superficial thrombophlebitis = topical heparinoid. (Book p1)

questions.q: The three phases of the surgical safety checklist, in order, are:
opts: Sign in → Time out → Sign out
Time out → Sign in → Sign out
Sign out → Sign in → Time out
Sign in → Sign out → Time out
questions.exp: The checklist flows Before induction of anaesthesia (sign in) → Before skin incision (time out) → Before patient leaves the operating room (sign out). (Book p2)

questions.q: 'Before induction of anaesthesia' (ward to OT complex) corresponds to which phase?
questions.exp: Sign in happens before induction of anaesthesia, in the ward to OT complex. (Book p2)

questions.q: 'Before skin incision' corresponds to which phase?
questions.exp: Time out is performed before skin incision. (Book p2)

questions.q: 'Before patient leaves the operating room' corresponds to which phase?
questions.exp: Sign out is completed before the patient leaves the operating room. (Book p2)

questions.q: During sign in, the patient has confirmed all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: At sign in the patient has confirmed identity, site (marked), procedure and written consent. (Book p2)

questions.q: Which of the following is checked during sign in?
questions.exp: Sign in includes known allergies and the risk of >500 ml blood loss. (Book p2)

questions.q: During sign in, the risk of blood loss greater than how much is assessed?
questions.exp: Sign in assesses the risk of >500 ml blood loss. (Book p2)

questions.q: During time out, the team confirms:
opts: Patient site, procedure name and time
questions.exp: Time out confirms patient site, procedure name and time. (Book p2)

questions.q: At time out, antibiotic prophylaxis must have been given within the last:
questions.exp: Time out checks that antibiotic prophylaxis was given within the last 30 min. (Book p2)

questions.q: During time out, the anticipated blood loss is estimated by the:
questions.exp: Anticipated blood loss at time out is given by the surgeon (actual loss at sign out is by the anaesthetist). (Book p2)

questions.q: During sign out, which of the following is verified?
questions.exp: Sign out verifies instruments, sponge and needle count. (Book p2)

questions.q: Specimen labelling during sign out must include:
questions.exp: Sign out includes specimen labelling (including patient name). (Book p2)

questions.q: During sign out, the actual blood loss is documented by the:
questions.exp: Actual blood loss at sign out is recorded by the anaesthetist. (Book p2)

questions.q: The note on the surgical safety checklist states that:
opts: There is no time in phase
questions.exp: The book's note: 'There is no time in phase' — time out is a pause in workflow, not a timed interval. (Book p2)

questions.q: The actual amount of blood loss is estimated as:
opts: Dry mop weight − wet mop weight
questions.exp: Actual amount = blood in suction − irrigation fluid. (Book p2)

questions.q: Alternatively, blood loss is estimated as:
opts: Wet mop weight − dry mop weight
Wet mop weight + dry mop weight
Dry mop weight − wet mop weight
questions.exp: Blood loss can also be estimated as wet mop weight − dry mop weight. (Book p2)

questions.q: A soaked mop represents a blood loss of:
questions.exp: Soaked mop = 100 cc of blood. (Book p2)

questions.q: A fist full of clots represents a blood loss of:
questions.exp: Fist full of clots = 500 cc of blood. (Book p2)

questions.q: Surgical mops carry a radio-opaque line so that they can be:
questions.exp: Mops have a radio-opaque line that is picked up on X-ray. (Book p2)

questions.q: The four OT zones are:
questions.exp: OT zoning = 1. Protective zone, 2. Clean zone, 3. Aseptic zone, 4. Disposal zone. (Book p2)

questions.q: Which of the following belongs to the protective zone?
opts: Change rooms, transfer bay, pre & post op rooms, ICU/PACU
questions.exp: Protective zone = change rooms, transfer bay, pre & post op rooms and ICU/PACU. (Book p2)

questions.q: The clean zone connects the protective zone to the:
questions.exp: The clean zone connects the protective zone to the aseptic zone. (Book p2)

questions.q: The equipment store room and maintenance workshop are in the:
questions.exp: Clean zone = equipment store room and maintenance workshop. (Book p2)

questions.q: The aseptic zone of the OT complex is the:
questions.exp: Aseptic zone = OT itself. (Book p2)

questions.q: The m/c position used for abdominal and breast surgeries is the:
questions.exp: Supine/neutral position is the m/c position used for abdominal and breast surgeries. (Book p3)

questions.q: The Trendelenberg position (head end low, foot end up) is used in:
questions.exp: Trendelenberg position is used in pelvic surgeries. (Book p3)

questions.q: The reverse Trendelenberg position is used in:
questions.exp: Reverse Trendelenberg is used in upper abdominal surgeries and in laparoscopic cholecystometry with right side up. (Book p3)

questions.q: In laparoscopic cholecystectomy, reverse Trendelenberg is taken with the:
questions.exp: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy uses reverse Trendelenberg with right side up. (Book p3)

questions.q: In laparoscopic cholecystectomy, CO2 collects below the right dome of the diaphragm, producing the m/c complication of:
questions.exp: CO2 collects below the right dome of diaphragm → right shoulder tip pain, the m/c complication. (Book p3)

questions.q: Lithotomy position is used in all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Lithotomy is used for obstetric, gynecologic, urologic (TURP) and hemorrhoid surgeries — not posterior cranial fossa surgery. (Book p3)

questions.q: The urologic procedure performed in lithotomy position mentioned in the book is:
questions.exp: Urologic procedures (TURP) are listed under the uses of lithotomy position. (Book p3)

questions.q: In lithotomy position, if the legs are not supported properly, the nerve commonly injured is the:
questions.exp: Nerve injured if legs are not supported properly: common peroneal nerve. (Book p3)

questions.q: The lateral (kidney) position is NOT used for:
questions.exp: Lateral/kidney position uses: thoracotomy, pyelolithotomy, nephrolithotomy, nephrectomy and breast reconstruction (latissimus dorsi flap). (Book p3)

questions.q: A breast reconstruction operation performed in the lateral (kidney) position uses the:
questions.exp: Breast reconstruction in the lateral position uses the latissimus dorsi flap. (Book p3)

questions.q: In the lateral (kidney) position, the increased risk of brachial plexus injury is due to:
questions.exp: Lateral position carries increased risk for brachial plexus injury d/t hyperextended arm. (Book p3)

questions.q: The prone position is used for:
opts: Spinal surgery and pilonidal sinus surgery
questions.exp: Prone position uses: spinal surgery and pilonidal sinus surgery. (Book p4)

questions.q: The sitting / Fowler's position is used for:
questions.exp: Sitting/Fowler's position is used for posterior cranial fossa surgery. (Book p4)

questions.q: An advantage of the sitting / Fowler's position is:
opts: Bloodless field with reduced blood loss
questions.exp: Advantages of Fowler's: ↓ blood loss (blood less field) and ↑ exposure. (Book p4)

questions.q: A disadvantage of the sitting / Fowler's position is:
questions.exp: Disadvantage of sitting/Fowler's position: ↑ risk of air embolism. (Book p4)

questions.q: The jackknife position is:
opts: Obsolete, previously used for hemorrhoid/fissure surgeries
The m/c position for abdominal surgery
Used for posterior cranial fossa surgery
questions.exp: Jackknife position = obsolete position, previously used for hemorrhoid fissure surgeries. (Book p4)

questions.q: A complication of the jackknife position is:
questions.exp: Complication of the jackknife position = positional asphyxia. (Book p4)

questions.q: The Lloyd-Davis position is a combination of:
questions.exp: Lloyd-Davis position = Trendelenberg + lithotomy position. (Book p4)

questions.q: The Lloyd-Davis position is used in:
questions.exp: Lloyd-Davis position is used in rectal cancer surgery. (Book p4)

questions.q: As per the book, how much air sucked into a vein enters circulation and dysregulates cardiac functioning?
questions.exp: Air (50-100cc) sucked into vein → enters circulation → dysregulates cardiac functioning. (Book p4)

questions.q: Air embolism is a risk in which of the following?
questions.exp: Risk factors for air embolism: thyroid/head & neck surgeries and sitting/Fowler's position. (Book p4)

questions.q: The m/c presenting feature of an air embolism is:
questions.exp: Clinical features: sudden desaturation, dyspnea and hypotension. (Book p4)

questions.q: Clinical features of air embolism include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Features = sudden desaturation, dyspnea, hypotension — fever is not listed. (Book p4)

questions.q: To prevent air embolism in the Fowler's position, the vein should be:
questions.exp: Prevention: 1. Ligate vein before cutting. (Book p5)

questions.q: Air entry into the field is further prevented by:
questions.exp: Prevention of air embolism in Fowler's position: ligate vein before cutting and irrigate field. (Book p5)

questions.q: Management of an air embolism begins with placing the patient in the:
questions.exp: Management starts with the Durant position, followed by aspiration of air. (Book p5)

questions.q: The Durant position consists of:
opts: Right side up (left lateral) + legs up
questions.exp: Durant position = right side up (left lateral) + legs up. (Book p5)

questions.q: After the Durant position, air is removed by:
opts: Aspiration using direct puncture / central line
questions.exp: Durant position is followed by aspirating air using direct puncture/central line. (Book p5)

questions.q: The Durant position is used when:
opts: Suspicion of air embolism is positive
The patient is bleeding into shock
questions.exp: The Durant position is used if suspicion of air embolism is (+). (Book p5)

questions.q: An adverse event is defined as:
opts: An incident that results in harm to the patient
An incident that could have harmed the patient
An incident that never reaches the patient
questions.exp: Adverse event = an incident that results in harm to the patient. (Book p5)

questions.q: A near miss is an incident that:
opts: Could have caused unwanted consequences but did not
Reaches the patient and causes injury
questions.exp: Near miss = an incident that could have resulted in unwanted consequences but did not. (Book p5)

questions.q: A near miss is prevented from reaching the patient by:
questions.exp: A near miss does not reach the patient either by chance or through timely intervention. (Book p5)

questions.q: A no-harm event:
opts: Reaches the patient but results in no injury
Is by definition an adverse event
questions.exp: No-harm event = an incident that occurs and reaches the patient but results in no injury. (Book p5)

questions.q: In a no-harm event, harm is avoided by:
questions.exp: In a no-harm event, harm is avoided by chance or due to mitigating circumstances. (Book p5)

units.title: Consents: Components & Signatures
units.guide: A valid consent covers identification, diagnosis, the planned procedure, the surgeon, description, patient-specific and procedure-specific complications (any complication >1% incidence), benefits and the alternate procedure — signed by patient, surgeon and witness.

units.title: IV Lines: Color-Coding of Cannulas
units.guide: From narrow to wide: yellow 24G (13/10 ml/min), blue 22G (31/30), pink 20G (67/60), green 18G (96), gray 16G (236/240) and orange 14G (270) — the orange 14G is the shock cannula. The 24G/22G/20G trio is bracketed for paediatric patients.

units.title: IV Lines: Superficial Thrombophlebitis
units.guide: The m/c IV complication is superficial thrombophlebitis — a tender, cord-like swelling at the cannulation site, managed with a topical heparinoid.

units.title: Safety Checklist: Phases & Sign In
units.guide: The checklist runs sign in (before induction of anaesthesia, ward to OT complex) → time out (before skin incision) → sign out (before the patient leaves the OT). Sign in confirms identity, marked site, procedure, written consent, known allergies and risk of >500 ml blood loss.

units.title: Safety Checklist: Time Out & Sign Out
units.guide: Time out confirms patient site, procedure name and time, checks antibiotic prophylaxis within the last 30 min and the surgeon's anticipated blood loss. Sign out verifies instruments/sponge/needle count, specimen labelling with patient name and the anaesthetist's actual blood loss — and the book's note: there is no time in phase.

units.title: Estimating Blood Loss
units.guide: Actual blood loss = blood in suction − irrigation fluid, or wet mop weight − dry mop weight. A soaked mop holds 100 cc, a fist full of clots 500 cc, and mops carry a radio-opaque line so they are picked up on X-ray.

units.title: OT Zoning: The Four Zones
units.guide: The OT complex flows through four zones: protective (change rooms, transfer bay, pre & post op rooms, ICU/PACU), clean (equipment store room, maintenance workshop — connecting protective to aseptic), aseptic (the OT itself) and disposal.

units.title: OT Positions: Supine, Trendelenberg & Reverse Trendelenberg
units.guide: Supine/neutral is the m/c position for abdominal and breast surgeries. Trendelenberg (head low, feet up) serves pelvic surgery; reverse Trendelenberg with right side up is used in laparoscopic cholecystectomy, where CO2 pools under the right diaphragm dome and causes right shoulder tip pain — its m/c complication.

units.title: OT Positions: Lithotomy & Lateral (Kidney)
units.guide: Lithotomy serves obstetric, gynecologic, urologic (TURP) and hemorrhoid procedures — with the common peroneal nerve at risk if legs are poorly supported. Lateral/kidney position covers thoracotomy, pyelo/nephrolithotomy, nephrectomy and breast reconstruction (latissimus dorsi flap), risking brachial plexus injury from a hyperextended arm.

units.title: OT Positions: Prone, Fowler's, Jackknife & Lloyd-Davis
units.guide: Prone is for spinal and pilonidal sinus surgery. Sitting/Fowler's exposes the posterior cranial fossa in a bloodless field but invites air embolism. Jackknife — once used for hemorrhoid/fissure surgery — is obsolete, killing by positional asphyxia. Lloyd-Davis = Trendelenberg + lithotomy, the rectal cancer position.

units.title: Air Embolism: Features, Prevention & Management
units.guide: 50-100 cc of air sucked into a vein dysregulates cardiac function; watch for it in thyroid/head & neck surgery and in Fowler's position. Sudden desaturation, dyspnea and hypotension are the clues — prevent by ligating the vein before cutting and irrigating the field, and treat with the Durant position (right side up/left lateral + legs up) followed by aspiration via direct puncture/central line.

units.title: Events in Patient Safety
units.guide: An adverse event harms the patient; a near miss could have but didn't (stopped by chance or timely intervention); a no-harm event reaches the patient without injury, harm dodged by chance or mitigating circumstances.
